newsitem.title: USA: Workers recover wreckage from Michigan plane crash.
newsitem.headline: Workers recover wreckage from Michigan plane crash.

text.p: Sheriff's deputies used snowmobiles and all-terrain vehicles Wednesday to reach the wreckage of a Cessna 210 airplane that crashed Tuesday night in a wooded recreation area west of Detroit, killing two executives from a Wisconsin paper company.

Menasha Corp of Neenah, Wis., said Donald Riviere, 57, a vice president for strategic development, and John Snyder, 49, a group president of the firm's material handling operations, died in the crash.

The men were returning to Wisconsin after a business-related trip to Madison Heights, Mich., where a Menasha subsidiary, Wolpac Inc., designs engineering products for the auto industry, said Menasha Corporate Vice President Jim Saraosiek.
Both men were licensed pilots, said Saraosiek, but it was unclear who was piloting the chartered plane when it went down.

The plane took off from Oakland-Troy airport Tuesday about 6 p.m. EST, police said. Witnesses told police they heard an airplane engine sputtering about 6:15 p.m. EST, then the engine picked back up before it fell silent.

Police were forced to call off their search about 10:45 p.m. EST Tuesday because of rainy weather and poor visibility that made it dangerous for searchers combing the lakes and swamps where the plane went down.

Police said it appeared the pilot may have been looking for a place to make an emergency landing before the six-passenger, single-engine airplane hit trees and crashed in the snow. Wreckage was strewn over a mile-wide area, police estimated.
A spokeswoman at the National Transportation Safety Board's regional office in West Chicago, Ill., said an inspector was scheduled to arrive on the scene Wednesday afternoon.
Menasha is a diversified manufacturing company whose principal businesses are paper and material handling. Saraosiek said the two men were part of the firm's executive team.

"But because our company is highly decentralized, almost all of our operations are highly autonomous. On a short-term basis, we can continue to manage. Long-term their contributions and presence will be missed," he said.

It was the second fatal airplane crash in Michigan in nearly two weeks. A Comair commuter plane crashed in southeastern Michigan Jan. 9, killing all 29 people aboard. Investigators have not yet determined the cause of that crash.
